```python
>>> pool.urlopen('GET', '/a')
<urllib3.response.HTTPResponse object at 0x700dd1f3d570>
```

vs.

```python
>>> pool = urllib3.PoolManager().connection_from_host('127.0.0.1', port=8000, scheme='http')
>>> pool.urlopen('GET', 'http://127.1.2.3/bb')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/krab/workspace/urllib3/src/urllib3/connectionpool.py", line 721, in urlopen
    raise HostChangedError(self, url, retries)
urllib3.exceptions.HostChangedError: HTTPConnectionPool(host='127.0.0.1', port=8000): Tried to open a foreign host with url: http://127.1.2.3/bb
```

In the example above (`urllib3.PoolManager().urlopen(method="GET", url="http://127.0.0.1:10000//v:h")`), the `PoolManager.urlopen` parses the URL. ℹ️ The first parse succeeds and correctly parses `//v:h` into `path`. Then, `HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen` is called with the URL of `//v:h` and it tries to parse the (path part of) URL again and fails. Probably correctly, because `h` is not a number of port.

Therefore, the fix should take into account the interplay between PoolManager and HTTPConnectionPool. A quick fix would be to add another parameter that would tell `HTTPConnectionPool` that the URL should not be parsed again because it's in fact only a path. Such change would be backwards compatible but there's already a ton of parameters.

I'm tagging also @shazow and @jalopezsilva because @sigmavirus24 has "Taking a break from FOSS" in his status line. It seems @shazow is the original author from long time ago and @jalopezsilva committed 691679f738ae098ce024aeae90cfdd8013b8e1e7 that added the unconditional `parse_url` call to `HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen`.

Do you see an option to avoid re-parsing the path?

comments.author: shazow
comments.body:
> The API of HTTPConnectionPool is slightly confusing. It uses the url parameter to mean two things. 

The way it was designed originally is through a layered approach: Each of the lower level layers is unaware of the higher level layers (HTTPConnection -> HTTPConnectionPool -> PoolManager etc).

Traditionally we prefer to do whatever input mangling in the highest layer possible, to allow for falling back to lower layers when necessary.

But I'm not very up to date on recent changes, cc @SethMichaelLarson @pquentin who are the current lead maintainers. :)

comments.author: crabhi
comments.body: Yeah, the problem is in the double parsing of the URL _using the same code_. The first pass parses `http://127.0.0.1:10000//v:h` correctly. Then, `//v:h` is sent again to `parse_url` and it fails.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
We got another drive-by PR in Requests about this so I took a look again. I think the solution is actually a lot simpler than we were thinking the last time I dug into this. The second `parse_url` is exclusively for scheme parsing for proxy support. We don't even use the parsed result when the path starts with a `/`, so we can completely sidestep it.

I have full details in https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/4952.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body:
> I'm also worried about how this is handled in when handling redirects in the retry logic (e.g., server returns a Location: //v:h or Location: //host:port//v:h but I haven't investigated that

Also this case is broken. This PR doesn't change anything about those semantics though. I don't know how common this is in practice since it's never been raised in either repo.

comments.author: nateprewitt
comments.body: This should be resolved in the next release with #3352. Then we can cleanup the patch in Requests. I'm going to close this out since the underlying issue is resolved. If we want to dig into the redirect case more, I think that's probably its own issue.

title: Workaround the error and make a request after migration to urllib3 >2. Multiprocessing is corrupted.
need_summary: The developer needed a way to bypass the DH_KEY_TOO_SMALL SSL error after upgrading to urllib3 >2, and the answer provides a concrete workaround using urllib3.util.create_urllib3_context with specific ciphers, demonstrated to work with urllib3 2.0.1 (see comment c1 code snippet).
security_topic: SSL handshake failure workaround after urllib3 upgrade
question_text: How can I make requests to problematic sites and work around errors after migrating to urllib3 >2?
answer_text:
This code works:
```python
import ssl
import requests
import urllib3

ctx = urllib3.util.create_urllib3_context(ciphers=':HIGH:!DH:!aNULL', cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_NONE)
adapter = requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter()
adapter.init_poolmanager(connections=2, maxsize=2, block=False, ssl_minimum_version=ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1, ssl_context=ctx)
requests_future = requests.Session()
requests_future.mount('https://', adapter)

print(requests_future.get("https://nhl.ru"))
```

comments.body:
I tested the above code on Android/Termux python3.11 (same **error** when using **multiprocessing**, but **threads work**).

I found a workaround:
$ /etc/ssl/openssl.cnf
CipherString = DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=2 -> CipherString = DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=1
Then multiprocessing does not cause an error.

Any ideas on how to use multiprocessing without editing 'openssl.cnf'? Let me remind you that in previous versions of urllib3 the hack urllib3.util.ssl_.DEFAULT_CIPHERS += ':HIGH:!DH:!aNULL' worked. Now it is broken and the proposed alternative does not work _(It would be more correct to say that it only works for threads, not processes.)._

broken processes (Replace processes with threads and the code will work (replace the line executor1 = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) -> executor1 = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)))
```python
import ssl
import urllib3

from urllib3 import PoolManager
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

executor1 = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)

ctx = urllib3.util.create_urllib3_context(ciphers=':HIGH:!DH:!aNULL', cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_NONE)
http = urllib3.PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx)

a = []
b = executor1.submit(http.request, "GET", "https://nhl.ru/")

a.append(b)

for i in a:
    print(i.result().status)
```

**Please respond to the developers, or the problem will be closed due to the impossibility of feedback.**

A year and updates later. The problem is not fixed.
**Python3.8-3-3.11, GNU/Linux (Debian Android/Termux)
urllib3::2.2.3
requests::2.32.3**


```python
import ssl
import requests
import urllib3
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

executor1 = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) # executor1 = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) #working

ctx = urllib3.util.create_urllib3_context(ciphers=':HIGH:!DH:!aNULL', cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_NONE)
```

title: fix for AIX ImportError: urllib3 v2.0 only supports OpenSSL 1.1.1+
need_summary: The developer asked if there is a fix for urllib3 v2.0 on AIX 7.3, and the maintainer answered that urllib3 v2.0 requires OpenSSL 1.1.1+ (or OpenSSL 3), citing the OpenSSL version requirement as the security anchor.
security_topic: required OpenSSL version for urllib3 v2.0 on AIX
question_text: is there a fix available for AIX 7.3?
answer_text:
Hello,

As mentioned on Discord, this issue is not specific to AIX in any way. To use urllib3 v2.0, you need OpenSSL 1.1.1+ as older versions of OpenSSL are no longer supported by the OpenSSL project and are likely to contain security issues, unless specifically patched. (OpenSSL 1.1.1 support was dropped by the OpenSSL project this month, so it's even better to switch to OpenSSL 3 if possible).

title: OpenSSL ERRORS on windows 10 desktops ==> require the "official solution"
need_summary: The developer needed a solution for the OpenSSL version error, and the maintainer answered that upgrading to a supported Python version (e.g., 3.7.17) resolves it, citing the Python versions documentation.
security_topic: compatibility of urllib3 v2.0 with OpenSSL on legacy Python 3.7
question_text:
I get the following error when trying to run some code that connects to a secure web-api
|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
**ImportError: urllib3 v2.0 only supports OpenSSL 1.1.1+, currently the 'ssl' module is compiled with 'OpenSSL 1.1.0i  14 Aug 2018'. See: https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/2168**
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I am running this on a windows 10 PC - there is no relevant advice in the "migration guide" located at:
 "https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/2168 " 
- my python version is 3.7.1
answer_text: Hello, Python 3.7 has reached end-of-life and is no longer receiving security updates: https://devguide.python.org/versions/. Your specific version (3.7.1) is five years old now. If you can't switch to a more recent version right away, at least try installing 3.7.17 instead. In any case, this is not a bug in urllib3 itself, so I'll close this issue. You can reach out to our community Discord if you have more questions.

You can reach out to [our community Discord](https://discord.gg/urllib3) if you have more questions.

title: Behavior change: v2.x raises SSLEOFError with Python3.10 where v2.x does not with Python3.8
need_summary: The developer needed to know why urllib3 v2 raises SSLEOFError on Python 3.10 due to the OpenSSL default cipher suite change, and the maintainer pointed to the change in the release notes/PR #2082 (https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/2082) and explained the cipher’s weakness.
security_topic: SSLEOFError regression caused by default cipher suite changes in urllib3 v2 with Python 3.10
question_text: Behavior change: v2.x raises SSLEOFError with Python3.10 where v2.x does not with Python3.8
answer_text:
Can you please try the following script to see if things improve?

```
import ssl

from urllib3 import PoolManager
from urllib3.util import create_urllib3_context

ctx = create_urllib3_context()
ctx.load_default_certs()
ctx.set_ciphers("AES256-SHA256")

with PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx) as pool:
    pool.request("GET", "https://.../", retries=0)
```

Also, would you mind sharing a full trackeback instead of just the exception?

(see https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3060#issuecomment-1576826956 and https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/2082)
thread_text:
ISSUE #3100: Behavior change: v2.x raises SSLEOFError with Python3.10 where v2.x does not with Python3.8
Author: b-morgenthaler
Date: 2023-08-01T10:34:19Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
### Subject

Setup: Using _robotframework-requests_ library which in turn utilizes _requests_ library to issue GET requests to a non-public web server over https. The web server is third-party.
The GET requests work fine using Python3.8, openssl [1.1.1f|3.0.2] and urllib3 2.x
The GET requests, however, raise following error when using the same context with only Python changed to 3.10:

`SSLError: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='10.1.1.32', port=443): Max retries exceeded with url: /netio.json (Caused by SSLError(SSLEOFError(8, 'EOF occurred in violation of protocol (_ssl.c:1007)')))`

### Environment

Reproduced on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and 22.04 LTS (openssl 1.1.1f and openssl 3.0.2)

Combination of libs that raise the error (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Python 3.10.12
OpenSSL 3.0.2 15 Mar 2022
urllib3 2.0.4
```
Combination of libs that do **not** raise the error (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Python 3.10.12
OpenSSL 3.0.2 15 Mar 2022
urllib3 1.26.15
```
Difference between the two combinations:
`pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall urllib3==1.26.15`

Combination of libs that do **not** raise the error as well (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.29
Python 3.8.10
OpenSSL 1.1.1f  31 Mar 2020
urllib3 2.0.4
```

### Steps to Reproduce

It's hard to reproduce publicly because the web server is not public.
But my findings lead to the SSL_OP_IGNORE_UNEXPECTED_EOF flag.

### Expected Behavior

v2.x shall behave the same way with Python 3.10 as it does with Python 3.8 regarding the error described above (i. e. not raising any SSLEOFError)

### Actual Behavior

v2.x in combination with Python 3.10 raises SSLEOFError
v2.x in combination with Python 3.8 does not raise SSLEOFError



--- COMMENTS ---

[c7] @sigmavirus24 2023-08-08T10:02:29Z:

> Could it be possible that the server is using the particular cipher suite because I chose to create the self-signed certificate as RSA SHA256?

No. The key used for a certificate is orthogonal to the cipher suites supported by the server for TLS.

I would also expect any product you purchase to allow you to customize the supported cipher suites so that you could fix this there.

Yes, we mentioned in the release notes that we would now be using the OpenSSL default cipher suite instead of the custom list in 1.26.x: see https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/2082. If you squint a bit, this is similar to a good cryptography practice: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothing-up-my-sleeve_number. What was surprising here is that you did not report an SSL handshake error, but an SSLEOFError. (Which is why I'd like to see the full traceback.)

That said, you're the fourth user reporting us an issue with the OpenSSL cipher suite, so we will likely need to reevaluate it and add more ciphers to it. Other reports include:

```
AES256-SHA256                  TLSv1.2 Kx=RSA      Au=RSA   Enc=AES(256)               Mac=SHA256
```

To rule out any side effects between OpenSSL versions (1.1.1f and 3.0.2) I ran my experiments from above in a plain ubuntu:focal (openssl 1.1.1f) and ubuntu:jammy (openssl 3.0.2) Docker container - both with Python 3.8 and 3.10.

`openssl/now 1.1.1f-1ubuntu2.19 amd64 [installed,local]`
`openssl/now 3.0.2-0ubuntu1.10 amd64 [installed,local]`

I did not change any of openssl's default configuration bundled with the official Ubuntu Docker image. I only install Python and some Python libraries additionally.

I can confirm that the output from `openssl ciphers -s -v DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=2` for both versions includes

`AES256-SHA256                  TLSv1.2 Kx=RSA      Au=RSA   Enc=AES(256)               Mac=SHA256`

comments.author: b-morgenthaler
comments.body:
### Subject

Setup: Using _robotframework-requests_ library which in turn utilizes _requests_ library to issue GET requests to a non-public web server over https. The web server is third-party.
The GET requests work fine using Python3.8, openssl [1.1.1f|3.0.2] and urllib3 2.x
The GET requests, however, raise following error when using the same context with only Python changed to 3.10:

`SSLError: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='10.1.1.32', port=443): Max retries exceeded with url: /netio.json (Caused by SSLError(SSLEOFError(8, 'EOF occurred in violation of protocol (_ssl.c:1007)')))`

### Environment

Reproduced on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and 22.04 LTS (openssl 1.1.1f and openssl 3.0.2)

Combination of libs that raise the error (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Python 3.10.12
OpenSSL 3.0.2 15 Mar 2022
urllib3 2.0.4
```
Combination of libs that do **not** raise the error (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Python 3.10.12
OpenSSL 3.0.2 15 Mar 2022
urllib3 1.26.15
```
Difference between the two combinations:
`pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall urllib3==1.26.15`

Combination of libs that do **not** raise the error as well (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS):
```
OS Linux-5.4.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.29
Python 3.8.10
OpenSSL 1.1.1f  31 Mar 2020
urllib3 2.0.4
```

### Steps to Reproduce

It's hard to reproduce publicly because the web server is not public.
But my findings lead to the SSL_OP_IGNORE_UNEXPECTED_EOF flag.

### Expected Behavior

v2.x shall behave the same way with Python 3.10 as it does with Python 3.8 regarding the error described above (i. e. not raising any SSLEOFError)

### Actual Behavior

v2.x in combination with Python 3.10 raises SSLEOFError
v2.x in combination with Python 3.8 does not raise SSLEOFError

Thanks! This is great. I still need to analyze things more to understand the EOF error, but the server is using the `TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256` cipher suite (named `AES256-SHA256` by OpenSSL) which is not in the OpenSSL default suite that we use in 2.0 (see https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/3060#issuecomment-1576826956 for details). Can you please try the following script to see if things improve?

```
import ssl

from urllib3 import PoolManager
from urllib3.util import create_urllib3_context

ctx = create_urllib3_context()
ctx.load_default_certs()
ctx.set_ciphers("AES256-SHA256")

with PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx) as pool:
    pool.request("GET", "https://.../", retries=0)
```

A little bit of background: the server is similar to this demo from its manufacturer: http://netio-4c.netio-products.com/
In our specific case, I am automating its JSON endpoint via SSL (self-signed). Could it be possible that the server is using the particular cipher suite because I chose to create the self-signed certificate as RSA SHA256?

I had to modify your script a bit because of the self-signed certificate (see below) but other than that, it is working. Unfortunately, I cannot control how my "frontend" (aka robotframework-requests) is utilizing Python's requests library which is utilizing urllib3 to make requests. I can only control whether to verify certificates (which I don't) and to ignore warnings.

```python
import ssl

from urllib3 import PoolManager
from urllib3.util import create_urllib3_context
from urllib3 import ssl
from urllib3 import make_headers

ctx = create_urllib3_context()
ctx.check_hostname = False
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
ctx.load_default_certs()
ctx.set_ciphers("AES256-SHA256")

type = {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
auth = make_headers(basic_auth=f'read:[read password]')
headers = { **type, **auth }

with PoolManager(ssl_context=ctx) as pool:
    resp = pool.request("GET", "https://[IP]/netio.json", retries=0, headers=headers)
    print(resp.data)
```

> A little bit of background: the server is similar to this demo from its manufacturer: http://netio-4c.netio-products.com/
> Could it be possible that the server is using the particular cipher suite because I chose to create the self-signed certificate as RSA SHA256?

No. The key used for a certificate is orthogonal to the cipher suites supported by the server for TLS.

I would also expect any product you purchase to allow you to customize the supported cipher suites so that you could fix this there.

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
Yes, we mentioned in the release notes that we would now be using the OpenSSL default cipher suite instead of the custom list in 1.26.x: see https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/pull/2082. If you squint a bit, this is similar to a good cryptography practice: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothing-up-my-sleeve_number. What was surprising here is that you did not report an SSL handshake error, but an SSLEOFError. (Which is why I'd like to see the full traceback.)

That said, you're the fourth user reporting us an issue with the OpenSSL cipher suite, so we will likely need to reevaluate it and add more ciphers to it. Other reports include:

 * https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3059
 * https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3031
 * https://discord.com/channels/756342717725933608/1117661048477073470

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
> Is the cipher AES256-SHA256 uncommon/weak/deprecated?

Yes, it is weak because RSA does not support PFS and CBC mode is vulnerable to plaintext attacks. See https://ciphersuite.info/cs/TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256/ for more explanations. But it's included by default on Ubuntu or Fedora, so your operating system seems to be configured differently.

Indeed, when I make requests from my Fedora laptop, this cipher is included. And looking at https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/openssl, running `openssl ciphers -s -v DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=2` confirms that Ubuntu includes it too:

```
AES256-SHA256                  TLSv1.2 Kx=RSA      Au=RSA   Enc=AES(256)               Mac=SHA256
```

How is your OpenSSL configured? It seems to be stricter than that, and you'll need to fix it.

> What was surprising here is that you did not report an SSL handshake error, but an SSLEOFError. (Which is why I'd like to see the full traceback.)

Looking more closely at the packet capture with Wireshark, I now understand why you got `SSLEOFError`. Looking at the relevant packets for one attempt:

| No. | Time | Source | Destination | Protocol | Length | Info |
| - | - | - | - | -| - | - |
|1 | 0.000000 | 172.17.0.2 | 10.1.1.32 | TCP | 74 | 47572 → 443 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0 MSS=1460 SACK_PERM TSval=12523148 TSecr=0 WS=128|
|2 | 0.000519 | 10.1.1.32 | 172.17.0.2 | TCP | 74 | 443 → 47572 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=5792 Len=0 MSS=1460 SACK_PERM TSval=566170005 TSecr=12523148 WS=4|
|3 | 0.000543 | 172.17.0.2 | 10.1.1.32 | TCP | 66 | 47572 → 443 [ACK] Seq=1 Ack=1 Win=64256 Len=0 TSval=12523149 TSecr=566170005|
|4 | 0.001904 | 172.17.0.2 | 10.1.1.32 | TLSv1 | 583 | Client Hello|
|5 | 0.002399 | 10.1.1.32 | 172.17.0.2 | TCP | 66 | 443 → 47572 [ACK] Seq=1 Ack=518 Win=6864 Len=0 TSval=566170005 TSecr=12523150|
|6 | 0.002935 | 10.1.1.32 | 172.17.0.2 | TCP | 66 | 443 → 47572 [FIN, ACK] Seq=1 Ack=518 Win=6864 Len=0 TSval=566170005 TSecr=12523150|
|7 | 0.002986 | 172.17.0.2 | 10.1.1.32 | TCP | 66 | 47572 → 443 [FIN, ACK] Seq=518 Ack=2 Win=64256 Len=0 TSval=12523151 TSecr=566170005|
|9 | 0.003338 | 10.1.1.32 | 172.17.0.2 | TCP | 66 | 443 → 47572 [ACK] Seq=2 Ack=519 Win=6864 Len=0 TSval=566170005 TSecr=12523151|

(I don't understand why Wireshark is reporting TLSv1 here, since urllib3 2.0 defaults to TLS 1.2 and the "Handshake Protocol Version" in Wireshark (not shown here) is TLS 1.2.)

Anyway, you can see that the client sends a Client Hello TLS frame in packet 4. While the server receives that packet, it then close the TCP connection in packet 6, which the client acknowledges. It's a violation of the protocol, instead an `Alert` should have been sent first, as seen in the Packet 6 below:

title: Urllib3 changes the case of hex letters in percent encodings
need_summary: The developer asked whether urllib3 should avoid normalizing percent‑encoded hex case for security testing, and the maintainer answered that urllib3 follows RFC 3986 which requires uppercase hex digits and will not change this behavior, citing the RFC as the source.
security_topic: percent-encoding case normalization policy
question_text: Is this normalization required for auth section? If so, we should only remove it for path, query and fragment, but keep it for auth.
answer_text:
We're following RFC 3986 when we normalize percent-encoded bytes and we likely won't change this position, even adding an option to do so doesn't feel right. The website that you're accessing should be conforming to the specification.

From RFC 3986 Section 2.1:

> For consistency, URI producers and normalizers should use uppercase hexadecimal digits for all percent-encodings.

title: No way to perform request for raw urls
need_summary: The developer asked whether urllib3 can send raw malformed URLs (a potential security vulnerability), and the maintainer answered that urllib3 isn’t suited for this and referenced the urllib3 connection‑pool documentation and Python’s http.client docs as the source.
security_topic: sending raw malformed URLs via urllib3
question_text: Please provide a way to set raw urls that will not be transformed implicitly
answer_text:
I looked a bit closer. We don't rely on the output `parse_url` in `HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen()` as long as the URL correctly starts with `/`. And in all cases we percent-encode invalid characters, indeed. So you can query `/../../foo/bar` but not an URL without a starting slash or invalid characters.

I don't think urllib3 is the right tool to use if you want to query malformed URLs. What you call a necessity could also be considered a vulnerability. Have you tried using https://docs.python.org/3/library/http.client.html instead?

title: urllib3 with version 2.0.* treats control character differently
need_summary: The change in urllib3 2.0 defaults to UTF‑8 encoding for string bodies (instead of Latin‑1), causing Content‑Length differences, as explained with links to the urllib3 request utility code (e.g., src/urllib3/util/request.py#L214‑L217) and the relevant RFC sections (RFC 2616, RFC 9110).
security_topic: difference in string body encoding causing Content-Length mismatch
question_text: The problem is after version 2.0.0, if you have control characters in your request body, urllib3 will count/treat them differently than previous version.
answer_text:
Indeed, `\x80` and `\x81` are outside of the 7-bit range, so they get represented using two bytes with UTF-8:

```python3
>>> len("test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81".encode("utf-8"))
12
>>> len("test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81".encode("latin1"))
9
```

## 1.26.x vs 2.0

urllib3 1.26.x relies on the standard library to encode `str` bodies, see https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/03ad6624c2b4a30cccf6d5b7e2b9999e104444ae/Lib/http/client.py#L1362-L1365. It uses the iso-8859-1 encoding.

urllib3 2.0 does its own encoding:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b63cc4c4868dadf1545ad9c5c189096532148a7d/src/urllib3/util/request.py#L214-L217

Since no encoding is provided to `to_bytes`, it will call `str.encode()`, and the default encoding there is UTF-8: https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.encode.
thread_text:
ISSUE #3053: urllib3 with version 2.0.* treats control character differently
Author: XiangFrank
Date: 2023-05-30T22:35:33Z
Labels: Contributor Friendly ♥, 💰 Bounty $100
State: closed

[c0]
### Subject

The problem is after version 2.0.0, if you have control characters in your request body, urllib3 will count/treat them differently than previous version.

For control characters like '\x08', '\x01', urllib3 after version 2.0.0 and before will count them into different bytes, which might cause the Content-Length mismatch in some cases.

### Environment

The environment I have is Python3.10, and I found this bug exists in all 2.0.* versions.

### Steps to Reproduce

This bug is easy to be reproduced. Here is a sample code I used:

```python
import urllib3

poolmanager = urllib3.PoolManager(num_pools=10, maxsize=3, block=False)
conn = poolmanager.connection_from_url("https://httpbin.org")
resp = conn.urlopen(method="POST", url="/post", body='test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81',  headers={
                                 'User-Agent': 'python-api/2', 'Accept-Encoding': 'gzip, deflate', 'Accept': '*/*', 'Connection': 'keep-alive'})
print(resp._body)
```

Run this code under different version of urllib3 (in my case, I used ver 1.26.6 and 2.0.2 for testing) you will find the 'Content-Length' of the response is totally different.

### Expected Behavior

The response body of the request under two different versions of urllib3 should be the same.

### Actual Behavior

The 'Content-Length' for ver 1.26.6 is 9 bytes, but for ver 2.0.2, it is 12 bytes.


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @sethmlarson 2023-05-31T03:02:56Z:
You're right that something changed, I believe this is caused by us favoring `utf-8` encoding of strings in v2.0 instead of `latin-1` in v1.26.x.
---
[c2] @Ousret 2023-05-31T03:17:21Z:
About that,
There is a miss at https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b63cc4c4868dadf1545ad9c5c189096532148a7d/src/urllib3/util/request.py#L230
StringIO objects still are Latin-1 encoded.
We want to consider adding a proper `Content-Type` when someone passes `str` as a body. Or the opposite, someone passes str but precise the Content-Type with specific _valid_ encoding.
---
[c3] @pquentin 2023-05-31T13:30:10Z:
Indeed, `\x80` and `\x81` are outside of the 7-bit range, so they get represented using two bytes with UTF-8:

```python3
>>> len("test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81".encode("utf-8"))
12
>>> len("test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81".encode("latin1"))
9
```

## 1.26.x vs 2.0

urllib3 1.26.x relies on the standard library to encode `str` bodies, see https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/03ad6624c2b4a30cccf6d5b7e2b9999e104444ae/Lib/http/client.py#L1362-L1365. It uses the iso-8859-1 encoding.

urllib3 2.0 does its own encoding:

https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/b63cc4c4868dadf1545ad9c5c189096532148a7d/src/urllib3/util/request.py#L214-L217

Since no encoding is provided to `to_bytes`, it will call `str.encode()`, and the default encoding there is UTF-8: https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.encode. (This seems quite implicit, it would be clearer to call `to_bytes` with the `utf-8` encoding).

## RFC 2616 vs RFC 91110

The standard library cites RFC 2616 Section 3.7.1 as a justification for using ISO-8859-1. Indeed, it states:

> The "charset" parameter is used with some media types to define the character set ([section 3.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-3.4)) of the data. When no explicit charset parameter is provided by the sender, media subtypes of the "text" type are defined to have a default charset value of "ISO-8859-1" when received via HTTP. Data in character sets other than "ISO-8859-1" or its subsets MUST be labeled with an appropriate charset value. See [section 3.4.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-3.4.1) for compatibility problems.

RFC 2616 is now obsolete, I believe the relevant RFC is RFC 9110. Per https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-content-type, here is the current recommendation:

> The "Content-Type" header field indicates the media type of the associated representation: either the representation enclosed in the message content or the [selected representation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#selected.representation), as determined by the message semantics. The indicated media type defines both the data format and how that data is intended to be processed by a recipient, within the scope of the received message semantics, after any content codings indicated by [Content-Encoding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#field.content-encoding) are decoded.
>
>     Content-Type = media-type
>
> Media types are defined in [Section 8.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#media.type). An example of the field is
>
>     Content-Type: text/html; charset=ISO-8859-4
>
> A sender that generates a message containing content SHOULD generate a Content-Type header field in that message unless the intended media type of the enclosed representation is unknown to the sender. The media type is indeed unknown to us so we should not send a Content-Type. And nothing specifies the default encoding anymore, so I suppose using UTF-8 is OK, and it's up to the recipient to realize that I think? And of course UTF-8 is just the better encoding here. It is well designed, can encode all of Unicode and is the [dominant encoding on the web](https://w3techs.com/technologies/cross/character_encoding/ranking).

But that's still a breaking change. If we want to keep it, we should mention it in the release notes. (And be consistent, as mentioned in https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/3053#issuecomment-1569436645 we sometimes continue using ISO-8859-1.)

comments.author: XiangFrank
comments.body:
### Subject

The problem is after version 2.0.0, if you have control characters in your request body, urllib3 will count/treat them differently than previous version.

For control characters like '\x08', '\x01', urllib3 after version 2.0.0 and before will count them into different bytes, which might cause the Content-Length mismatch in some cases.

### Environment

The environment I have is Python3.10, and I found this bug exists in all 2.0.* versions.

### Steps to Reproduce

This bug is easy to be reproduced. Here is a sample code I used:

```python
import urllib3

poolmanager = urllib3.PoolManager(num_pools=10, maxsize=3, block=False)
conn = poolmanager.connection_from_url("https://httpbin.org")
resp = conn.urlopen(method="POST", url="/post", body='test\x80\x80\x01\x01\x81',  headers={
                                 'User-Agent': 'python-api/2', 'Accept-Encoding': 'gzip, deflate', 'Accept': '*/*', 'Connection': 'keep-alive'})
print(resp._body)
```

Run this code under different version of urllib3 (in my case, I used ver 1.26.6 and 2.0.2 for testing) you will find the 'Content-Length' of the response is totally different.

The response body of the request under two different versions of urllib3 should be the same.

### Actual Behavior

The 'Content-Length' for ver 1.26.6 is 9 bytes, but for ver 2.0.2, it is 12 bytes.

title: [REG 1.26.15 -> 2.0.2] SSLV3_ALERT_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE
need_summary: The developer asked why a TLS handshake fails when using a weak cipher with urllib3 2.0, and the maintainer explained that urllib3 2.0 relies on the system OpenSSL cipher configuration and advised configuring the exact ciphersuite or OpenSSL, referencing urllib3 v2.0.
security_topic: TLS handshake failure with weak cipher suite in urllib3 v2.0
question_text: It should connect. If I allow ECDH (by removing `:!ECDH`), the negotiated cipher is `ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384`, and connection succeeds. This might be intended, but I didn't find it documented anywhere.
answer_text: urllib3 v2.0 uses whatever the system (or OpenSSL's) configured cipher suites are by default. My guess is that your OpenSSL is configured to use non-weak ciphers, so when the handshake happens there is no overlap between the client and server. The work-around is to either configure the exact ciphersuite you need in urllib3 or to configure your OpenSSL to allow a weaker ciphersuite (not recommended, as it would impact all applications).

comments.body:
urllib3 v2.0 uses whatever the system (or OpenSSL's) configured cipher suites are by default. My guess is that your OpenSSL is configured to use non-weak ciphers, so when the handshake happens there is no overlap between the client and server. The work-around is to either configure the exact ciphersuite you need in urllib3 or to configure your OpenSSL to allow a weaker ciphersuite (not recommended, as it would impact all applications).

Going to close this as I believe this is the issue you're facing, if there's additional information we can reopen this issue.

title: urllib3>=2.0 does not work with system Python on macOS
need_summary: Developers needed to know if urllib3 works with macOS system Python using LibreSSL, and the maintainer answered that it is only a warning and can be resolved by using urllib3 2.0.3 or newer (or pinning to <2), see the version‑specific guidance in the comments.
security_topic: urllib3 compatibility with LibreSSL on macOS system Python
question_text: What are you recommending to macOS users that do not want to or are not allowed to use a Homebrew version of Python?
answer_text: We've already relaxed the restriction from an error to a warning in the latest versions of urllib3 2.x. We won't be removing the warning, it's up to users to either move to a Python compiled with OpenSSL or be okay with running in an untested configuration. If you're seeing an error and accept the risks of running an untested configuration then you can upgrade to the latest urllib3.
thread_text:
ISSUE #3020: urllib3>=2.0 does not work with system Python on macOS
Author: andy-maier
Date: 2023-05-08T10:01:41Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Subject

The system Python on macOS 12.6.5 is Python 3.9.6 whose ssl module is compiled with LibreSSL 2.8.3.

The removal of LibreSSL support in urllib3 2.0 makes it impossible to be used with the system Python on macOS.

What are you recommending to macOS users that do not want to or are not allowed to use a Homebrew version of Python?

In our Python packages that use requests / urllib3, we will now either have to pin urllib3 to <2.0, or have to have a trouble shooting documentation for how to deal with that.

At the least, I think urllib3 should add some trouble shooting info on how to find out what the Python ssl module is compiled with, and the options to deal with the issue.

Note that issue #2168 misses one important case: The user created a virtualenv based on the system Python. Using a virtualenv makes it possible and reasonable to install packages from Pypi. That is how a macOS user gets into the problem of using a Python that was compiled with LibreSSL and uses urllib3>=2.0.

That is the case that issue describes as "The combination of the above three is very unlikely.", but that is exactly how it happens and I don't think it is unlikely. There is no rule (that I know of) that prevents or discourages from using the system Python for a virtualenv, and then to install packages from Pypi.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-08T11:47:45Z:
While true, CPython is removing support for compiling against Libressl so it's unlikely to be the case long term. 
---
[c2] @andy-maier 2023-05-08T12:06:47Z:
Note that [PEP-644](https://peps.python.org/pep-0644) lists macOS in its OpenSSL section as "macOS (python.org installer)" and does not show the system Python provided in macOS at all, which uses LibreSSL up to Ventura. IMO, that PEP should have listed "macOS (system Python)" in its LibreSSL section as well.

Considering the use of the system Python on macOS, the statement in PEP-644 "No macOS and Windows user will be affected by the deprecation." is simply not true. There are environments where you simply don't have the choice to install another Python version.

So if urllib3 refers to PEP-644, it should also be aware of the fact that that PEP seems to ignore the use of the system Python on macOS.

If I look at the situation from an end user perspective, then the PSF apparently ignores what Apple does, and urllib3 follows that and also ignores it. That is not helpful for Python users on macOS.

If you take a look at https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/issues/2168, then the meanwhile larger part of its comments (at least when measured as vertical screen size) are from the last 4 days where users started to realize the incompatibilities.
---
[c3] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-08T12:30:29Z:
The system python on macOS is actively recommended against by most resources I'm aware. It's there for macOS tooling and development (software developed by Apple).I believe the PSF has no sway over language decisions so you want to blame the Steering Council for accepting the PEP. (Although, really wildly accusing other humans who volunteer to work on a project like Python of malicious intent or incompetence is really shitty behavior regardless of whether you address the right group or not.)

The reality is that Python offers dmg files for macOS users that are complied against openssl and there are other options like asdf(, pyenv, etc.) for local user installation and homebrew.

If you're looking to blame someone for incompatibilities, look to the Libressl project. They forked hard. Between Google's boringssl, Libressl, and openssl the APIs are too different for one person (the only person willing to maintain `ssl`) who does the maintenance entirely in their free time. (At least that's my guess - that it's too much to be able to be confident in the secure usage of the various APIs).

It's not a great place to be, I agree, but regardless of whether this library checks that or not, Libressl is not going to be well supported and likely not trustable within Python on any platform that compiles against it. There will be patches used to make it compile and likely those will be carried forward until something makes it hard to get those to work or a CVE is found in the fragile integration. 
---
[c4] @andy-maier 2023-05-08T12:33:44Z:
> Although, really wildly accusing other humans who volunteer to work on a project like Python of malicious intent or incompetence is really shitty behavior regardless of whether you address the right group or not.

I did not intend to accuse anyone (and don't think I did), and particularly not the great folks that lead the development of Python. I just pointed out a particular single-sidedness of that PEP w.r.t. macOS, where it seems to assume that people don't use the system Python, while the PEP does not do that for any of the other OSs listed there.
---
[c5] @andy-maier 2023-05-08T12:37:40Z:
I have the same feelings about LibreSSL as you expressed, but with Apple choosing that library, the situation has become more difficult. That decision has given LibreSSL a certain weight.
---
[c6] @andy-maier 2023-05-08T12:39:07Z:
Do you have a link to where Apple states that the system Python in macOS has the restricted purpose you stated above?
---
[c7] @andy-maier 2023-05-08T12:53:05Z:
I think I'm not really arguing for python or urllib3 supporting LibreSSL.

But the problem this causes for macOS users should be more appreciated, IMO. That's why I suggested adding trouble shooting info.
---
[c8] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-08T13:01:25Z:
> Do you have a link to where Apple states that the system Python in macOS has the restricted purpose you stated above?

Apple doesn't state that explicitly but if you file a radar about something with system python and your development against it, they generally close those (is what I've heard over the last decade of being involved in the community). I've never filed a radar so I can't speak to it myself.

> Apple choosing that library, the situation has become more difficult. That decision has given LibreSSL a certain weight.

I agree it's definitely complicates a lot of things. That said, Apple also has hard forked bash to 3.x because 4.x adopted GPLv3 iirc and so Apple's built-in software isn't designed for users in these cases but to protect Apple from legal issues. Previously the openssl that was on macOS was ancient and heavily patched by Apple. There used to be guides that recommended brew installing a newer openssl and python to avoid the problems with it (no SNI, old cipher suites, iirc).

I'm on my phone so it is far more difficult to compile a list of citations for you, but I don't believe the community advice should be that difficult to find either. It was in most books, I think even some of the libraries had documentation around this. I think the python-guide recommended (possibly still does) against system python. 
---
[c9] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-08T13:05:28Z:
> But the problem this causes for macOS users should be more appreciated, IMO

I agree. I think there are discussions happening around this. The difficult bit is that we want to be confident in the security we provide for users and we rely on `ssl` for that.

I think that the SC probably discussed this issue but I as someone who noticed the PR, didn't think of macOS users (even though I use it at work) I suspect for the same reason that other folks didn't - most of us use non-system python. 
---
[c10] @sthen 2023-05-09T09:14:51Z:
> While true, CPython is removing support for compiling against Libressl so it's unlikely to be the case long term.

That's not what was proposed in the OpenSSL PEP and it is not what has happened. CPython is no longer adding workarounds for libressl-related things (so a passive "not going out of its way to support it") but the PEP clearly says that it's not taking an active step of rejecting compiling against LibreSSL.

Specifically, what I see that's been changed in 3.10 in this area is removal of what are mostly workarounds for obsolete LibreSSL versions that are no longer useful anyway (and may even get in the way - we've found that to be the case fairly often with other software).
---
[c11] @pquentin 2023-05-09T10:05:54Z:
Thanks for your excellent points. We might revisit our decision, but need to investigate more. That said, I wanted to answer to one specific question.

> Do you have a link to where Apple states that the system Python in macOS has the restricted purpose you stated above?

Yes, see the macOS 10.15 release notes: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-catalina-10_15-release-notes#Scripting-Language-Runtimes

> ## Scripting Language Runtimes
> ### Deprecations
> 
> * Scripting language runtimes such as Python, Ruby, and Perl are included in macOS for compatibility with legacy software. Future versions of macOS won’t include scripting language runtimes by default, and might require you to install additional packages. If your software depends on scripting languages, it’s recommended that you bundle the runtime within the app. (49764202)
>  * Use of Python 2.7 isn’t recommended as this version is included in macOS for compatibility with legacy software. Future versions of macOS won’t include Python 2.7. Instead, it’s recommended that you run python3 from within Terminal. (51097165)

Python 2.7 was then [officially deprecated in macOS 12.0](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-12_0_1-release-notes#Python) and [removed in macOS 12.3](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-12_3-release-notes). https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/95284 acknowledged this.

There's no more "system Python": Python 3 is now installed only if you install the Xcode Command Line Tools, and is meant for LLDB scripting, as described in the [LLVM docs](https://lldb.llvm.org/resources/caveats.html) and the [Xcode 13 release notes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode-release-notes/xcode-13-release-notes) which state:

> * LLDB’s Python scripting no longer supports Python 2. (73956573)


---
[c12] @pquentin 2023-05-10T07:55:29Z:
Even though the "system Python" is only installed with developer tools and is only meant for scripting a debugger when using Xcode, I realize this is hurting users.

We mentioned that we were following the lead of PEP 644, but:

 * I don't think this Xcode Python existed when the PEP was written in October 2020?
 * The wording in the PEP is harsh, but even CPython is not actively dropping LibreSSL, see https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/28728 for example. (Patches are still needed on Gentoo though: https://github.com/gentoo/libressl/tree/master/dev-lang/python/files)
 * Unlike Gentoo which already patched urllib3, users hitting the LibreSSL issue on macOS are often new to Python, and this is not welcoming.
 * cryptography dropped support for OpenSSL<1.1.1, but they still actively support LibreSSL

Should we open the door to LibreSSL? One issue is that LibreSSL 2.8.3 was released in December 2018 and has been EOL since December 2019. Still, my opinion is that **requiring** OpenSSL is harsh and a warning should be enough for users that are not using OpenSSL for now.

@sethmlarson @sigmavirus24 What do you think?
---
[c13] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-10T13:07:35Z:
I am on board with relaxing the restriction. I'm only worried about debugging Libressl problems if they come up when it's not something we can easily support or test against and the support provider will likely be per-downstream.

What do folks think about something like what requests has to provide additional debugging info in the bug template? 
---
[c14] @pquentin 2023-05-10T13:47:36Z:
> What do folks think about something like what requests has to provide additional debugging info in the bug template?

Good idea. requests has https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/Bug_report.md which asks to run `python -m request.help` which is quite comprehensive, but we have https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/02_bug_report.md and I can extend it to print `ssl.OPENSSL_VERSION` which gives `OpenSSL 3.0.8 7 Feb 2023` on my Linux laptop and `LibreSSL 2.8.3` on my Macbook.




---
[c15] @sethmlarson 2023-05-10T14:00:59Z:
I'm also on board with relaxing the restriction to allow any version of LibreSSL as long as we explicitly emit a warning that LibreSSL isn't supported and continue to raise an error for non-OpenSSL/LibreSSL implementations. The unfortunate thing is I'm unsure how we are going to test that whatever we've done is at least correct initially for us to feel comfortable releasing it at all, anyone have ideas how to get an authentic Python build that uses LibreSSL?
---
[c16] @mistermocha 2023-05-10T22:00:56Z:
Hey I came across this, and I do the bulk of my work in virtual environments. My newly created venv picks up the ssl module from whatever-the-system-ssl-module is.

It took lots of digging to figure out that if I install openssl1.1.1 from homebrew, blow away my bin folder in my venv, then recreate my venv entirely, it links the ssl package properly. 

I'm happy to document the process for those that are having trouble if someone can point me to the right place for it,

[c17] @sigmavirus24 2023-05-10T22:09:52Z:
@mistermocha thanks for the offer! I don't believe that documentation belongs in urllib3. If you're already using homebrew, I would just install Python from that, not try to have openssl work with XCode Python. There are other opinionated guides like https://docs.python-guide.org/starting/install3/osx/#install3-osx that exist for this express purpose. Alternatively, you could write a blog post about this. Documentation isn't just in the official repository for any open source project. Sometimes the best documentation is someone describing how they solved a problem in their own words on their own blog
---

It was: Apple had begun shipping a Python 3 linked against LibreSSL with their Command Line Tools and Xcode when Catalina was released in October 2019, first previewed in June 2019.

Apple doesn't state that explicitly but if you file a radar about something with system python and your development against it, they generally close those (is what I've heard over the last decade of being involved in the community). I've never filed a radar so I can't speak to it myself.

> Apple choosing that library, the situation has become more difficult. That decision has given LibreSSL a certain weight.

I agree it's definitely complicates a lot of things. That said, Apple also has hard forked bash to 3.x because 4.x adopted GPLv3 iirc and so Apple's built-in software isn't designed for users in these cases but to protect Apple from legal issues. I'm on my phone so it is far more difficult to compile a list of citations for you, but I don't believe the community advice should be that difficult to find either. I agree. I think there are discussions happening around this. The difficult bit is that we want to be confident in the security we provide for users and we rely on `ssl` for that.

comments.author: sthen
comments.body:
> While true, CPython is removing support for compiling against Libressl so it's unlikely to be the case long term.

That's not what was proposed in the OpenSSL PEP and it is not what has happened. CPython is no longer adding workarounds for libressl-related things (so a passive "not going out of its way to support it") but the PEP clearly says that it's not taking an active step of rejecting compiling against LibreSSL.

Specifically, what I see that's been changed in 3.10 in this area is removal of what are mostly workarounds for obsolete LibreSSL versions that are no longer useful anyway (and may even get in the way - we've found that to be the case fairly often with other software).

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
Thanks for your excellent points. We might revisit our decision, but need to investigate more. That said, I wanted to answer to one specific question.

> Do you have a link to where Apple states that the system Python in macOS has the restricted purpose you stated above?

Yes, see the macOS 10.15 release notes: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-catalina-10_15-release-notes#Scripting-Language-Runtimes

> ## Scripting Language Runtimes
> ### Deprecations
> 
> * Scripting language runtimes such as Python, Ruby, and Perl are included in macOS for compatibility with legacy software. Future versions of macOS won’t include scripting language runtimes by default, and might require you to install additional packages. If your software depends on scripting languages, it’s recommended that you bundle the runtime within the app. (49764202)
>  * Use of Python 2.7 isn’t recommended as this version is included in macOS for compatibility with legacy software. Future versions of macOS won’t include Python 2.7. Instead, it’s recommended that you run python3 from within Terminal. (51097165)

Python 2.7 was then [officially deprecated in macOS 12.0](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-12_0_1-release-notes#Python) and [removed in macOS 12.3](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/macos-release-notes/macos-12_3-release-notes). https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/95284 acknowledged this.

There's no more "system Python": Python 3 is now installed only if you install the Xcode Command Line Tools, and is meant for LLDB scripting, as described in the [LLVM docs](https://lldb.llvm.org/resources/caveats.html) and the [Xcode 13 release notes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode-release-notes/xcode-13-release-notes) which state:

> * LLDB’s Python scripting no longer supports Python 2. (73956573)

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
Even though the "system Python" is only installed with developer tools and is only meant for scripting a debugger when using Xcode, I realize this is hurting users.

We mentioned that we were following the lead of PEP 644, but:

 * I don't think this Xcode Python existed when the PEP was written in October 2020?
 * The wording in the PEP is harsh, but even CPython is not actively dropping LibreSSL, see https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/28728 for example. (Patches are still needed on Gentoo though: https://github.com/gentoo/libressl/tree/master/dev-lang/python/files)
 * Unlike Gentoo which already patched urllib3, users hitting the LibreSSL issue on macOS are often new to Python, and this is not welcoming.
 * cryptography dropped support for OpenSSL<1.1.1, but they still actively support LibreSSL

Should we open the door to LibreSSL? One issue is that LibreSSL 2.8.3 was released in December 2018 and has been EOL since December 2019. Still, my opinion is that **requiring** OpenSSL is harsh and a warning should be enough for users that are not using OpenSSL for now.

@sethmlarson @sigmavirus24 What do you think?

comments.author: sigmavirus24
comments.body:
I am on board with relaxing the restriction. I'm only worried about debugging Libressl problems if they come up when it's not something we can easily support or test against and the support provider will likely be per-downstream.

What do folks think about something like what requests has to provide additional debugging info in the bug template?

comments.author: pquentin
comments.body:
> What do folks think about something like what requests has to provide additional debugging info in the bug template?

Good idea. requests has https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/Bug_report.md which asks to run `python -m request.help` which is quite comprehensive, but we have https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/02_bug_report.md and I can extend it to print `ssl.OPENSSL_VERSION` which gives `OpenSSL 3.0.8 7 Feb 2023` on my Linux laptop and `LibreSSL 2.8.3` on my Macbook.

title: Module 'urllib3.connectionpool' has no attribute 'VerifiedHTTPSConnection'
need_summary: The developer asked if the removal of urllib3.connectionpool.VerifiedHTTPSConnection is intentional and what the alternative is, and the maintainer answered that the alias still exists in urllib3 v2.0 under urllib3.connection.
security_topic: attribute relocation in urllib3 after upgrade
question_text:
With the latest urllib3 release we are seeing - 
`AttributeError: module 'urllib3.connectionpool' has no attribute 'VerifiedHTTPSConnection'`
Is this intentional? What is the alternative function?
answer_text: The alias still exists in urllib3 v2.0 but under `urllib3.connection`, not `connectionpool`. The code you're using was working by coincidence because the name was imported and used in a different module. If you fix this code to use `urllib3.connection` then everything will work as expected.

title: Deprecate schemeless URLs?
need_summary: The developer asked whether schemeless URLs should be deprecated/removed to avoid parsing ambiguities (a potential security risk), and the answer provides a concrete fork branch that removes support for schemeless URLs (https://github.com/JohnJamesUtley/urllib3/tree/remove_schemeless_urls).
security_topic: deprecation of schemeless URLs
question_text: Deprecate schemeless URLs?
answer_text: I think adding a `DeprecationWarning` as you mentioned that links to this issue (we can edit the issue body to provide actionable feedback for users) and says that a removal will occur in a future version. We can then get that released in 1.26.x and 2.x to start warning users and gathering feedback if necessary.
thread_text:
ISSUE #2920: Deprecate schemeless URLs?
Author: kenballus
Date: 2023-02-14T20:22:33Z
Labels: 💰 Bounty $300
State: closed

[c0]
### Context

Schemeless URLs can cause a lot of parsing confusion because they aren't standardized in the RFC. Examples like the following are especially weird, and could cause problems when interoperability with other parsers matters:
```
"evil.com://good.com"
```

Here are some popular URL parsers' interpretations:
urllib3:
```
Scheme:   (nil)
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     evil.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     //good.com
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

cpython urllib:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

furl:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

hyperlink:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     /
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

rfc3986:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

yarl:
```
Scheme:   evil.com
Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     /
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

As you can see, we're the outlier here.

In my opinion, this is something worth fixing, but I imagine that schemeless URLs are in pretty widespread use with urllib3. Thus, we might consider adding a DeprecationWarning that encourages people to explicitly state their schemes.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @sethmlarson 2023-02-14T21:20:38Z:
Totally agree that this is something worth fixing, thank you for doing all this research and opening this. My hope is that schemeless URLs aren't as widespread as we think and that we've been supporting this mostly for backwards compatibility and not because a large swath of the ecosystem relies on it.

I think adding a `DeprecationWarning` as you mentioned that links to this issue (we can edit the issue body to provide actionable feedback for users) and says that a removal will occur in a future version. We can then get that released in 1.26.x and 2.x to start warning users and gathering feedback if necessary.

```
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

rfc3986:
```

Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     (nil)
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

yarl:
```

Userinfo: (nil)
Host:     good.com
Port:     (nil)
Path:     /
Query:    (nil)
Fragment: (nil)
```

As you can see, we're the outlier here.

In my opinion, this is something worth fixing, but I imagine that schemeless URLs are in pretty widespread use with urllib3. Thus, we might consider adding a DeprecationWarning that encourages people to explicitly state their schemes.

security_topic: TLS cipher selection causing 403 response in urllib3
question_text: I have a strange issue where a request to a certain website gives error 403 using urllib3, but succeeds using urllib and curl.
answer_text:
Installing urllib3 from git got it working: `pip install git+https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3.git`

I was curious which commit in the 2.x.x branch fixed it, so I did some testing. This is the commit which changes the result from 403 to 200:
* 841a727 - Use system TLS ciphers if using OpenSSL 1.1.1+ or SecureTransport

My OpenSSL version was `OpenSSL 1.1.1n  15 Mar 2022`, so I presume that the server didn't accept the non-system ciphers...

I will try to use 2.0.0a3. The `requests` library requires an older version, but installing like this gets the `requests.get` to succeed:
```
RUN pip install requests
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3.git@2.0.0a3
```

Author: am-zq
Date: 2023-02-08T16:48:56Z

### Subject

Hello, I have a strange issue where a request to a certain website gives error 403 using urllib3, but succeeds using urllib and curl. The code is running in Docker using an official Python image. I have attempted to match the headers sent by urllib3 to the ones sent by urllib, however it still didn't succeed. The issue does not occur on the Docker host (which is an Ubuntu VM). 

### Environment

Docker image: python:3.10.6-bullseye
Platform: OS Linux-5.15.0-58-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.31
Python: Python 3.10.6
urllib3: urllib3 1.26.5

### Steps to Reproduce

Dockerfile and script to send a few test requests using urllib and urllib3 below. The specific package versions were to match the Docker host where the request is successful, but the latest versions installed by pip had the same issue.

**Dockerfile**
```
FROM python:3.10.6-bullseye

RUN apt-get update

RUN apt-get install -y openssl

RUN pip install requests==2.25.1 pyopenssl==21.0.0 urllib3==1.26.5 certifi==2020.6.20 cryptography==3.4.8

WORKDIR /code
COPY . .

CMD ["python3", "test.py"]
```

**docker-compose.yaml**
```
version: "3.9"
services:
  tests:
    build: .
```

**test.py**
```
import requests
import logging

import http.client as http_client
http_client.HTTPConnection.debuglevel = 1
logging.basicConfig()
logging.getLogger().setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

url = 'https://www.blackrock.com/uk'

print(">> NOW TRYING: urllib.request")
import urllib.request
handler = urllib.request.HTTPSHandler(debuglevel=1)
opener = urllib.request.build_opener(handler)
req = opener.open(url)

print(">> NOW TRYING: urllib3")
import urllib3
http = urllib3.PoolManager()
r = http.request('GET', url)
print(r.status)

print(">> NOW TRYING: urllib3 with headers and ordering matching urllib")
r = http.request('GET', url, headers={'Accept-Encoding': 'identity', 'Host': 'www.blackrock.com', 'User-Agent': 'Python-urllib/3.10', 'Connection': 'close'})
print(r.status)

```

### Expected Behavior

The request should succeed, as it does using urllib.

```
tests_1  | >> NOW TRYING: urllib.request
tests_1  | send: b'GET /uk HTTP/1.1\r\nAccept-Encoding: identity\r\nHost: www.blackrock.com\r\nUser-Agent: Python-urllib/3.10\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n'
tests_1  | reply: 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n'
...
```
Full output attached: [docker_urllib_test_output.txt](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/files/10687880/docker_urllib_test_output.txt)

### Actual Behavior
It returns a 403 error. Note that the `send: b'GET...` log line in the second attempt exactly matches the successful attempt from urllib above. I thought this would mean exactly the same bytes were being sent, but possibly something is being handled differently behind the scenes.
```
tests_1  | >> NOW TRYING: urllib3
tests_1  | DEBUG:urllib3.connectionpool:Starting new HTTPS connection (1): www.blackrock.com:443
tests_1  | send: b'GET /uk HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: www.blackrock.com\r\nAccept-Encoding: identity\r\nUser-Agent: python-urllib3/1.26.5\r\n\r\n'
tests_1  | reply: 'HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\n'
...
tests_1  | >> NOW TRYING: urllib3 with headers matching urllib
tests_1  | DEBUG:urllib3.connectionpool:Resetting dropped connection: www.blackrock.com
tests_1  | send: b'GET /uk HTTP/1.1\r\nAccept-Encoding: identity\r\nHost: www.blackrock.com\r\nUser-Agent: Python-urllib/3.10\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n'
tests_1  | reply: 'HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\n'
...
```

I have spent a few hours on this, but this is as far as I got with the debug logging. I get that this could potentially be a Docker issue, but the fact that urllib succeeds with the same request led me to post here. I'm happy to do some more testing if someone has suggestions for what else to try.

[c1] @am-zq 2023-02-10T16:55:02Z:
Installing urllib3 from git got it working: `pip install git+https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3.git`

I was curious which commit in the 2.x.x branch fixed it, so I did some testing. This is the commit which changes the result from 403 to 200:
* 841a727 - Use system TLS ciphers if using OpenSSL 1.1.1+ or SecureTransport

My OpenSSL version was `OpenSSL 1.1.1n  15 Mar 2022`, so I presume that the server didn't accept the non-system ciphers...

I will try to use 2.0.0a3. The `requests` library requires an older version, but installing like this gets the `requests.get` to succeed:
```
RUN pip install requests
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3.git@2.0.0a3
```

The warning from pip is:
```
requests 2.25.1 requires urllib3<1.27,>=1.21.1, but you have urllib3 2.0.0a3 which is incompatible.
```

Your docs say v2.0 has 99% functional API compatibility, so hopefully it will just work!

Is it worth merging that commit into 1.26.x branch so others don't run into this issue?
---
[c2] @sethmlarson 2023-02-10T17:53:55Z:
This is almost certainly the server filtering on something that urllib3 is doing like a User-Agent, TLS etc, but I can't tell you what that thing is since we don't have access to the server source code. Since this isn't a defect in the library itself I don't think there's much we can do here. Going to close this issue.

thread_text:
ISSUE #2893: InvalidChunkLength errors raised can't be pickled -> unpickled
Author: Tarty
Date: 2023-01-20T08:52:50Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Subject

The impacted application is using a concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor (and the library apscheduler) to schedule and execute a set of jobs. When one job is raising an error, the error instance is pickled to be retrieved by the main process that will unpickle it.

Lately, an API used as source for one of the job was not accessible anymore due to an internal DNS issue. This as expected led to the job raising an error.

However, instead of being handled as a job that failed, the main process crashed and the process pool was broken.

After having a look, it looks like the error raised by the job couldn't be pickled/unpickled, and that this was the cause of the main process crashing.

Here is the full traceback of the error raised by the job that tried to download data from the unavailable API:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 761, in _update_chunk_length
self.chunk_left = int(line, 16)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 16: b''

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 444, in _error_catcher
yield
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 828, in read_chunked
self._update_chunk_length()
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 765, in _update_chunk_length
raise InvalidChunkLength(self, line)
urllib3.exceptions.InvalidChunkLength: InvalidChunkLength(got length b'', 0 bytes read)

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/requests/models.py", line 816, in generate
yield from self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True)
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 624, in stream
for line in self.read_chunked(amt, decode_content=decode_content):
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 816, in read_chunked
with self._error_catcher():
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/contextlib.py", line 153, in __exit__
self.gen.throw(typ, value, traceback)
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/urllib3/response.py", line 461, in _error_catcher
raise ProtocolError("Connection broken: %r" % e, e)
urllib3.exceptions.ProtocolError: ("Connection broken: InvalidChunkLength(got length b'', 0 bytes read)", InvalidChunkLength(got length b'', 0 bytes read))
```

and the error in the main process that ensued:

```
concurrent.futures.process._RemoteTraceback:
'''
Traceback (most recent call last):
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/concurrent/futures/process.py", line 387, in wait_result_broken_or_wakeup
result_item = result_reader.recv()
File "/usr/local/lib/python3.10/multiprocessing/connection.py", line 251, in recv
return _ForkingPickler.loads(buf.getbuffer())
TypeError: InvalidChunkLength.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'length'
'''

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

concurrent.futures.process.BrokenProcessPool: A process in the process pool was terminated abruptly while the future was running or pending.
```


### Environment

Running in python 3.10.9-bullseye Docker image
Python 3.10.9
urllib3==1.26.14

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import pickle
from urllib3 import HTTPResponse
from urllib3.exceptions import InvalidChunkLength

error = InvalidChunkLength(HTTPResponse(), b'')
pickled = pickle.dumps(error)
pickle.loads(pickled)
```

### Expected Behavior

The above snippet wouldn't raise an error. An InvalidChunkLength error raised by urllib3 can be pickled an unpickled.

### Actual Behavior

The above snippet leads to the following error being raised:

```
In [1]: import pickle
   ...: from urllib3 import HTTPResponse
   ...: from urllib3.exceptions import InvalidChunkLength
   ...:
   ...: error = InvalidChunkLength(HTTPResponse(), b'')
   ...: pickled = pickle.dumps(error)
   ...: pickle.loads(pickled)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[1], line 7
      5 error = InvalidChunkLength(HTTPResponse(), b'')
      6 pickled = pickle.dumps(error)
----> 7 pickle.loads(pickled)

TypeError: InvalidChunkLength.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'length'
```

-----

Thank you for your time and attention!

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @sethmlarson 2023-02-05T19:58:16Z:
We don't test the picklability of any of our exception classes, if you'd be willing to contribute this without much of a problem I could see it being useful but since this is the first report in a long time about pickling exceptions I'm not sure how broad the need is.
---
[c2] @Dobatymo 2023-02-23T04:27:27Z:
I can reproduce this with `urllib3-1.26.14`, but not with the latest commit on main https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/commit/5e072876b81e8adb30df8cdffbc756b7af883ca4. I couldn't find the related change, but it might be fixed already.
---

Author: Jeff-Silverman
Date: 2023-01-04T19:33:25Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Context

What are you trying to do?
Several places I have worked have environmental variables, typically HTTP_PROXY or similar, which point to a proxy server.  Sending traffic through the proxy is required.  You may assume that the proxy is under the control of the cybersecurity organization.
How do you expect to do it?
Set up these envars in a bash script or windows
Is it something you currently cannot do?
Not with urllib3,  Request can do it.
Is this related to an existing issue/problem?
Not that I know of.


### Alternatives

Can you achieve the same result doing it in an alternative way?
Yes.  Use os.getenv to look for http_proxy, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY, and use those values as inputs to the urllib3.ProxyManager constructor.
Is the alternative considerable?
Yes.

### Duplicate

Has the feature been requested before?

title: `util.parse_url` allows invalid characters in reg-names
need_summary: Developer asked whether invalid characters in URL reg-names should be percent‑encoded or cause a parse failure; the maintainer referenced the WHATWG URL spec (e.g., https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point) indicating they should reject such characters.
security_topic: percent-encoding vs rejection of invalid characters in URL parsing
question_text: If someone tries to encode a URL containing an invalid character (e.g. `'�'`) in a reg-name, should we automatically percent-encode it, or should we reject the parse?
answer_text: Sorry for taking so long to get to this. I'm going to make a call that we continue doing what we're doing and percent-encode everything that's outside the valid ranges for each component. Can discuss more but I think it's better to make a call rather than delay indefinitely.
thread_text:
ISSUE #2802: `util.parse_url` allows invalid characters in reg-names
Author: kenballus
Date: 2022-11-13T04:40:33Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### `util.parse_url` allows invalid characters in reg-names.

RFC3986 defines reg-name as follows:
`reg-name = *( unreserved / pct-encoded / sub-delims )`
`unreserved = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~"`
`sub-delims = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")" / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="`
`pct-encoded = "%" HEXDIG HEXDIG`

Currently, `urllib3.util.parse_url` accepts reg-names containing characters outside those enumerated above.
The incorrectly accepted ASCII characters are `[\x00-\x20]`, `"`, `<`, `>`, `^`, `` ` ``, `{`, `|`, `}`, and `\x7f`.

### Environment
```python3
>>> print("OS", platform.platform())
OS Linux-6.0.7-arch1-1-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
>>> print("Python", platform.python_version())
urllib3 2.0.0.dev0
>>> print("urllib3", urllib3.__version__)
Python 3.10.8
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```python3
>>> import urllib3
>>> urllib3.util.parse_url("http://|") # Whatever happens, "|" should not end up in a reg-name.
Url(scheme='http', auth=None, host='|', port=None, path=None, query=None, fragment=None)
>>> # But it does!
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @kenballus 2022-11-13T17:08:40Z:
WHATWG also disallows many of these characters. Quoting the WHATWG spec:

"If input contains a [forbidden host code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error), return failure."
"A forbidden host code point is U+0000 NULL, U+0009 TAB, U+000A LF, U+000D CR, U+0020 SPACE, U+0023 (#), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003C (<), U+003E (>), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005B ([), U+005C (\), U+005D (]), U+005E (^), or U+007C (|)."
(If you see any of these characters, the parse should fail)

"If input contains a [code point](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) that is not a [URL code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-code-points) and not U+0025 (%), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error)."
"The URL code points are [ASCII alphanumeric](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-alphanumeric), U+0021 (!), U+0024 ($), U+0026 (&), U+0027 ('), U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS, U+0029 RIGHT PARENTHESIS, U+002A (*), U+002B (+), U+002C (,), U+002D (-), U+002E (.), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003B (;), U+003D (=), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005F (_), U+007E (~), and [code points](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) in the range U+00A0 to U+10FFFD, inclusive, excluding [surrogates](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#surrogate) and [noncharacters](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#noncharacter)."
(If you see any characters other than these characters, they will later be percent-encoded.)
---
[c2] @kenballus 2022-11-13T17:42:07Z:
> 3986 isn't the end of the line. WHAT WG supports Unicode ignoring 3987

The docs say "This parser is RFC 3986 and RFC 6874 compliant," so I would assume that RFC compliance trumps WHATWG compliance. Is that a safe assumption to make?

I'm not sure what Unicode has to do with this; this is about incorrectly accepted ASCII characters. The PR currently breaks Unicode, but that's pretty easily fixable, I just need to know which Unicode URL spec to comply with (RFC3987 or WHATWG).
---
[c3] @sethmlarson 2022-11-19T00:13:32Z:
@kenballus Yeah that's a safe assumption, we implement RFC 3986 instead of WHATWG. Why have you closed your PR btw?

```python3

OS Linux-6.0.7-arch1-1-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
>>> print("Python", platform.python_version())
urllib3 2.0.0.dev0
>>> print("urllib3", urllib3.__version__)
Python 3.10.8
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```python3
>>> import urllib3
>>> urllib3.util.parse_url("http://|") # Whatever happens, "|" should not end up in a reg-name.
Url(scheme='http', auth=None, host='|', port=None, path=None, query=None, fragment=None)
>>> # But it does!
```

comments.body:
WHATWG also disallows many of these characters. Quoting the WHATWG spec:

"If input contains a [forbidden host code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error), return failure."
"A forbidden host code point is U+0000 NULL, U+0009 TAB, U+000A LF, U+000D CR, U+0020 SPACE, U+0023 (#), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003C (<), U+003E (>), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005B ([), U+005C (\), U+005D (]), U+005E (^), or U+007C (|)."
(If you see any of these characters, the parse should fail)

"If input contains a [code point](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) that is not a [URL code point](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-code-points) and not U+0025 (%), [validation error](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#validation-error)."
"The URL code points are [ASCII alphanumeric](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-alphanumeric), U+0021 (!), U+0024 ($), U+0026 (&), U+0027 ('), U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS, U+0029 RIGHT PARENTHESIS, U+002A (*), U+002B (+), U+002C (,), U+002D (-), U+002E (.), U+002F (/), U+003A (:), U+003B (;), U+003D (=), U+003F (?), U+0040 (@), U+005F (_), U+007E (~), and [code points](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#code-point) in the range U+00A0 to U+10FFFD, inclusive, excluding [surrogates](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#surrogate) and [noncharacters](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#noncharacter)."
(If you see any characters other than these characters, they will later be percent-encoded.)

The docs say "This parser is RFC 3986 and RFC 6874 compliant," so I would assume that RFC compliance trumps WHATWG compliance. Is that a safe assumption to make?

I'm not sure what Unicode has to do with this; this is about incorrectly accepted ASCII characters. The PR currently breaks Unicode, but that's pretty easily fixable, I just need to know which Unicode URL spec to comply with (RFC3987 or WHATWG).
